claim: A demonstrated 'Clean Hard-Surface Sub-D Modeling' technique orders the stack as Crease/Weight the base mesh -> Subdivision Surface -> Bevel (Limit Method Weight, Harden Normals, after/below Subdivision) -- the REVERSE of this project's own standing policy (blender-modeling-technique-corrections.md #2: 'sharp edges get bevel weight + a Bevel modifier ordered BEFORE Subdivision Surface'). The video frames Bevel-after-SubD as specifically avoiding pinched/distorted shading on curved hard-surface hulls that a pre-SubD bevel can produce.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation (2026-08-15, Modifiers chapter pass, 1:07:24-1:42:01): at 76:09-77:57, the demonstrated stack order is Crease/Bevel-Weight on the base mesh, then Subdivision Surface (Ctrl+2), then a Bevel modifier UNDER/AFTER Subdivision with Limit Method Weight and Harden Normals -- explicitly contrasted against 'a traditional Sub-D workflow [that] often places Bevel before Sub-D.'
rejected_alternative: Silently adopting this order and overwriting the existing Bevel-before-SubD policy without reconciling why two credible sources disagree, or silently ignoring this source because it conflicts with an already-established project convention.
reason: This is a genuine, sourced disagreement with an existing standing policy, not a new topic -- it needs to be flagged and reconciled (likely: which order is correct probably depends on WHERE the bevel is used -- a physically-radiused edge that should read as round even far from camera vs. a crisp mechanical seam -- rather than one order being universally right), not silently resolved in either direction. Recorded as CAPTURED/CONFLICT rather than folded into the policy until an actual reconciliation pass or a controlled test (bevel-before-SubD vs. bevel-after-SubD on the same test edge, compared for pinching) is done.

claim: When different edge sets on the same object need different bevel segment counts/widths/profiles that a single Bevel modifier's one Limit Method (Angle or Weight) can't express together, stack multiple Bevel modifiers, each scoped to a different Vertex Group (Limit Method: Vertex Group) containing only that edge set's vertices.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 73:26-76:08, multiple Bevel modifiers are stacked, each set to Limit Method: Vertex Group, with loop cuts used where necessary to isolate the target vertices into separate vertex groups -- solving cases where a single global Angle/Weight limit can't express two genuinely different bevel treatments on one body.
rejected_alternative: A single Bevel modifier with one global width/segment setting applied uniformly via bevel-weight, forcing every weighted edge to share the same physical bevel radius even when reference photos show visibly different fillet sizes on different parts of the same object.
reason: Extends this project's existing single-Bevel-modifier-by-weight policy for cases with genuinely different bevel radii on one asset (e.g. a large primary silhouette rounding vs. a tight panel-seam chamfer) -- not yet needed on any built asset, but a real capability gap in the current typed op surface (add_modifier/set_modifier_parameter can already do this manually; no vertex-group-scoped-bevel convenience wrapper exists).

claim: A Weld modifier (small merge distance, ~0.01-0.05cm) inserted between a Boolean modifier and a subsequent Bevel modifier merges the near-coincident/zero-length edges a boolean cut leaves at its intersection boundary, which otherwise block Bevel's Clamp Overlap from expanding the fillet cleanly at that seam.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 77:58-80:05, stack order Boolean -> Weld (small distance) -> Bevel (Angle) is demonstrated specifically to clean up boolean-intersection microgeometry that would otherwise prevent the Bevel modifier from filleting the cut seam.
rejected_alternative: This project's current boolean workflow (add_modifier BOOLEAN, set operand/operation, apply, delete cutter) with no Weld or Bevel cleanup step afterward -- leaves cut seams sharp/unfilleted and potentially carrying boolean-artifact micro-geometry.
reason: Directly fills a stated gap: this project has never added a Weld modifier or a post-boolean Bevel to any built asset. Relevant the next time a boolean cut needs a filleted (not razor-sharp) seam -- e.g. a cast-metal object where boolean-cut edges should read as machined/rounded, not knife-edge.

claim: A Cube + Subdivision Surface + Cast modifier (Cast type: Sphere, Factor 1.0) produces an all-quad sphere with uniform topology, avoiding both the UV-Sphere's polar triangle-fan pinching and the Icosphere's uneven triangulation -- relevant whenever a spherical hard-surface part needs to be cleanly cut, beveled, or subdivided further (domes, ball joints, round housings).
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 95:52-97:51, a Quad Sphere (Cube -> Subdivision Surface -> Cast-to-Sphere Factor 1.0, or the built-in Add Mesh Extra Objects 'Round Cube') is directly contrasted with UV-Sphere polar pinching and Icosphere triangulation artifacts under further subdivision/beveling.
rejected_alternative: Blender's default UV Sphere or Icosphere primitives for any round hard-surface part that will later need holes cut or edges beveled -- both have topology defects (pole pinching, uneven triangle flow) that this project's own mesh-validity-vs-mesh-quality lesson says automated checks won't catch but wireframe/SubD inspection will.
reason: This project has not yet needed a true sphere primitive, but the next time one is needed (a rounded knob, a ball joint, a dome) this is the correct starting primitive rather than create_primitive('sphere', ...) as currently exposed, which likely wraps a UV-Sphere.

claim: A Shrinkwrap modifier set to Project mode, scoped to a Vertex Group containing only a secondary part's mounting-footprint verts, conforms that footprint flush against a curved host-body surface without manual boolean bridging or retopology -- the mounting rim deforms to match the host's curvature while the rest of the secondary part stays untouched.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 100:09-101:55, a sensor-mount's base rim is isolated into a Vertex Group, then a Shrinkwrap modifier (Project mode, local Z-axis) targets it at a curved body mesh, conforming only that footprint flush against the double-curved hull.
rejected_alternative: Manually sculpting/moving the mounting footprint's vertices by hand to match the host surface's curvature, or booleaning the two parts together and losing the ability to move the secondary part independently afterward.
reason: This is the same Shrinkwrap-based handle-snap mechanism flagged as an untested hypothesis in [[video-curriculum-mug-diagnosis]] for the mug's unresolved handle-attachment failure -- independent confirmation from a second source that vertex-group-scoped Shrinkwrap Project is a real, established technique for exactly this kind of problem (conforming one part's attachment footprint to another's curved surface), not a one-off guess. Raises confidence that this hypothesis is worth actually testing on the mug, not just noting as plausible.

claim: Enabling Bisect (and Flip if needed) on a Mirror modifier lets it be added to an already-asymmetric or already-applied mesh directly -- the modifier clips off the unwanted side and mirrors the kept side across the axis, instead of requiring the artist to manually delete half the mesh in Edit Mode first.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 82:40-83:56, Mirror modifier's Bisect option is enabled on an asymmetric/already-applied mesh, dynamically clipping and mirroring the desired side across the centerline without manual half-mesh deletion.
rejected_alternative: Manually selecting and deleting half the mesh in Edit Mode before adding a Mirror modifier -- destructive and hard to undo if the wrong half is deleted or the asset later needs to return to being asymmetric.
reason: A lower-risk way to add symmetry to an asset built without one from the start (e.g. recovering symmetry on a mesh edited unevenly by hand in the GUI), non-destructive and reversible by just disabling Bisect again.
